title: The Hidden Caching Bug That Can Wipe Out Your Entire Database Overnight — Engineering Cheat Sheet
subtitle: Prevent Cache Stampedes from inducing catastrophic cascading database failure.
summary: This bug occurs when a high-traffic cache key expires, causing concurrent requests to bypass the cache and overwhelm the underlying database. Without synchronization, this 'cache stampede' triggers a feedback loop that can exhaust connection pools and crash the storage layer.

key_concepts.name: Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd)
key_concepts.detail: A phenomenon where simultaneous requests for an expired cache key trigger multiple expensive database queries, leading to CPU exhaustion, increased latency, and potential service-wide database outages.

key_concepts.name: Probabilistic Early Recomputation
key_concepts.detail: A strategy using a decaying probability function to trigger cache refresh before expiration, ensuring only one worker updates the value while others serve stale data.

key_concepts.name: Mutex Locking (Distributed Lock)
key_concepts.detail: Utilizing distributed locks (e.g., Redis SET NX) to ensure only a single process executes the database query during a cache miss, forcing others to wait/retry.

code_cheatsheet.explanation: Bulk-clearing keys without caution causes an immediate stampede; always use Lua scripts or background jobs to stagger expiration times.
Implements probabilistic early recomputation to spread the load of cache updates, effectively smoothing out spikes in database traffic.

best_practices: Implement jittered expiration times to prevent multiple keys from expiring simultaneously.
Always use a distributed lock (mutex) on cache misses for expensive queries.
Configure aggressive database connection pooling and circuit breakers to isolate cache-related failures.
Implement stale-while-revalidate patterns to allow service continuity during database latency spikes.

interview_qa.question: How do you prevent a thundering herd problem when a globally accessed cache entry expires?
interview_qa.answer: Use probabilistic early recomputation or a distributed mutex (e.g., Redis lock) to ensure only one thread performs the re-fetch. This decouples the expiration event from the heavy compute task, protecting the database from concurrent request bursts.
